name: Backgammon
intro: Learn Backgammon step by step: the board, moving with the dice, hitting and the bar, bearing off, then strategy: the best opening moves, safe play, primes and the pip count.

units.name: How Backgammon works
units.blurb: The board, the dice, hitting and bearing off.

lessons.title: How to play Backgammon: the board and setup
lessons.summary: Backgammon in two minutes: the 24 points, where your 15 checkers start, which way they move and what your home board is.
lessons.wrap: Fifteen checkers, all heading home. Next: how the dice move them.

steps.text:
Backgammon is played on a board of 24 narrow triangles, called points. You have 15 gold checkers and your opponent has 15 ivory ones.

The points are numbered 1 to 24 from your side. Your checkers travel from the high numbers down towards point 1.
Points 1 to 6, at the bottom right, are your home board. Your goal is to bring all 15 checkers home, then take them off the board. That’s called bearing off.
steps.prompt: Tap all six points of your home board.
steps.wrong: Your home board is the bottom-right quarter: points 1 to 6.
steps.done: That’s home. The first player to bear off all 15 checkers wins.

steps.text: Your opponent moves the other way round the board, towards their own home board at the top right.
steps.prompt: Which way do your checkers move?
steps.explain: From 24 down to 1, then off the board.

lessons.title: Backgammon moves: using the dice
lessons.summary: How to move in Backgammon: each die moves one checker that many points, the two dice can move one checker or two, and doubles move four times.
lessons.wrap: Each die is its own move, and doubles count twice. Next: points you can’t land on.

steps.text:
On your turn you roll two dice. Each die is a separate move: one checker moves the number on one die, and one checker (the same or another) moves the number on the other.

To move, tap a checker, then tap the point it should go to. The bright outlines show where you can go.
You rolled 6 and 5.
steps.prompt: Play your 6 and your 5. Any legal move is fine.

steps.text: Rolling a double is special: you play the number four times.
steps.prompt: You rolled double 2. Make four moves of 2.

steps.text: One more rule: if you can play both dice, you must. If you can only play one, play the bigger one if you can.
steps.prompt: You roll 4 and 4. How many points can you move in total?

lessons.title: Backgammon hitting: blots and the bar
lessons.summary: In Backgammon a single checker is a blot. Land on one to hit it and send it to the bar, and learn how checkers come back in from the bar.
lessons.wrap: Hit lone checkers, and come in from the bar before anything else. Next: bearing off.

steps.text:
You can’t land on a point with two or more of your opponent’s checkers. That point is blocked, or made.

But a point with just one opposing checker, called a blot, is open. Land on it and you hit it: the blot goes to the bar in the middle and has to start again.
Ivory has left a blot on point 10.
steps.prompt: Hit the blot.
steps.wrong: Find a checker that can land exactly on point 10 with one of your dice.
steps.done: Hit! That checker has to go all the way back round.

steps.text:
Now one of your checkers is on the bar. Before you move anything else, it must come back in, on your opponent’s home board at the top right. A 1 enters on point 24, a 2 on 23, and so on down to a 6 on 19.

You rolled 6 and 4. Point 19 is blocked, so the 6 can’t bring it in.
steps.prompt: Bring your checker in from the bar, then play the other die.
steps.wrong: Tap your checker on the bar first. Only the 4 lands on an open point.
steps.done: Back in on point 21, then the 6 played elsewhere.

lessons.title: Backgammon bearing off: finishing the race
lessons.summary: Once all 15 of your checkers are home you can bear them off. Learn how the dice take checkers off, and what to do with a roll bigger than you need.
lessons.wrap: All home, then off by the dice. Next: a quick rules check.

steps.text:
When all 15 of your checkers are in your home board, you can start bearing off. A die takes a checker off from the point with that number: a 6 from the 6 point, a 4 from the 4 point.

To bear off, tap a checker, then tap the tray on the right.
steps.prompt: You rolled 6 and 4. Bear off two checkers.
steps.wrong: Use each die to take a checker off from the point with that number.

steps.text: If a die is higher than your highest checker, you can use it to bear off from your highest point.
steps.prompt: You rolled 6 and 5, but your highest checkers are on 3. Bear off two.
steps.wrong: A die bigger than you need bears off from your highest point.
steps.done: Both dice bear off from the 3 point.

steps.text: One more rule.
steps.prompt: You’re bearing off and one of your checkers gets hit. What happens?
options: It must come in from the bar and get home before you bear off again
steps.explain: It goes to the bar. It has to come back in and travel home before you can bear off any more.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Show you know the rules, then on to strategy.

lessons.title: Backgammon rules check
lessons.summary: A quick Backgammon rules check: hit a blot, then answer two questions about the bar and doubles. Pass it to move on to strategy.
lessons.wrap: Rules done. Now for the strategy that wins races and battles.

steps.text: Three questions. First, a move.
steps.prompt: Hit the ivory blot.

steps.text: Second.
steps.prompt: You have a checker on the bar. What must you do first?
options: Bring it in before any other move
Anything, as long as you bring it in this turn
Wait until it’s your opponent’s turn
steps.explain: A checker on the bar must come in before you move anything else.

steps.text: Last one.
steps.prompt: Can you land on a point with two of your opponent’s checkers?
options: Yes, and you hit them both
steps.explain: No. Two or more checkers make a point that you can’t land on.

units.name: Winning ideas
units.blurb: Opening moves, safety, primes and the race.

lessons.title: Backgammon opening moves: the best first rolls
lessons.summary: The best Backgammon opening moves for 3-1, 4-2 and 6-1: use the roll to make a new point in front of your home board.
lessons.wrap: With 3-1, 4-2 and 6-1, make a point. Next: staying safe from hits.

steps.text:
The best opening rolls let you make a point: put two checkers together on a new point, so it’s safe from hits and blocks your opponent.

The most valuable points to make early are your 5 point, your 4 point and your 7 point (the bar point).
3-1 is the best opening roll of all.
steps.prompt: Use 3-1 to make your 5 point.
steps.wrong: Bring one checker from 8 and one from 6 to land together.
steps.done: The 5 point. Strong players make it every time.

steps.text: 4-2 works the same way.
steps.prompt: Use 4-2 to make your 4 point.
steps.wrong: Which two checkers can both land on point 4?

steps.text: And 6-1 makes the bar point, right next to the bar.
steps.prompt: Use 6-1 to make your 7 point.
steps.wrong: One checker from 13 and one from 8 can meet on 7.
steps.done: Three points in a row: 8, 7 and 6. That’s the start of a wall.

lessons.title: Backgammon strategy: avoid leaving blots
lessons.summary: Single checkers, called blots, can be hit and sent back. Learn to count your blots and choose the play that keeps your checkers safe.
lessons.wrap: Play safe when you can. Next: building a prime.

steps.text:
Every blot is a risk. If your opponent rolls the number that reaches it, it gets hit and loses all the ground it had covered.

When you have a choice, prefer plays that leave no blots, or leave them where they’re hard to hit.
You have a blot on your 5 point and rolled 3-1.
steps.prompt: Play the roll so that no checker is left alone.
steps.wrong: That still leaves a blot somewhere. Try covering the 5 point.
steps.done: No blots, and the 5 point made too.

lessons.title: Backgammon strategy: building a prime
lessons.summary: A prime is a wall of points in a row that your opponent can’t get past. Learn why six points in a row traps their checkers completely.
lessons.wrap: Points in a row make a wall. Next: counting the race.

steps.text:
A prime is a row of made points next to each other. Your opponent’s checkers behind it can only jump as far as a die allows, and no die is bigger than 6.

Six points in a row, a full prime, can’t be passed at all. Here, ivory’s two checkers on your 1 point are trapped.
Check the idea.
steps.prompt: Why can’t ivory’s checkers get past six points in a row?
options: Because they’d need to move 7 or more in one hop
Because primes are a special rule
steps.explain: Each die moves one hop, and the most a die can show is 6. Every landing spot within reach is blocked, even with doubles.

lessons.title: Backgammon pip count: who is ahead in the race
lessons.summary: The pip count is the total distance your checkers must travel to bear off. Learn to count it and use it to decide whether to race or fight.
lessons.wrap: Count the race before you decide how to play. That’s the Backgammon path complete!

steps.text:
Each checker needs to travel its point number to bear off: a checker on 13 needs 13 pips. Add them all up and you have your pip count. Lower is better.

At the start, both players need 167: 2×24 + 5×13 + 3×8 + 5×6.
The game page shows both pip counts above the board.
steps.prompt: You need 120 pips and your opponent needs 145. Who’s ahead in the race?
steps.explain: You, by 25 pips. Fewer pips means fewer rolls to get home.

steps.text: Last question.
steps.prompt: You’re well ahead in the race. What should you usually do?
options: Get your checkers home safely and race
steps.explain: When you’re ahead, avoid contact: run home safely and bear off. Hitting and blocking matter more when you’re behind.
